title: Experimental Benchmarking of a 256-Qubit Room-Temperature NV-Diamond Quantum Processor with an Optically Programmable Biomolecular Quantum Bus
authors: Adams Ivanov, Daniela Herrmann, Erick Giovani Sperandio Nascimento
abstract: We report Zeus-256, a room-temperature nitrogen-vacancy (NV) diamond processor with 256 simultaneously active processor-level logical qubits arranged in a 16 x 16 array. Each logical qubit combines an NV electron-spin ensemble with nuclear-spin memory and ancillary resources. OpenQASM 2.0 circuits are transpiled into RFSoC-controlled microwave, radio-frequency, optical, timing, measurement and bus-configuration sequences. An optically programmable proprietary protein-chromophore layer with an internal metastable-triplet spin mediator provides a reconfigurable biomolecular quantum bus for local and long-range interactions. Benchmarks cover QFT, GHZ entanglement, Grover search, arithmetic, variational, neural-network, graph-state and Shor-family circuits. Factor recovery is reported for 11 integers of 8-84 bits, with 10 attempts per instance; the 84-bit endpoint uses 256 qubits and 40,250,342 reported gates, with a reported execution time of 551.694 ms. Bell-CHSH measurements yield S = 2.8008 +/- 0.0446. Three-qubit Grover search returns the marked state in 958 of 1,024 shots (93.55%), compared with an ideal reference of 94.53%. A separate 30,000-shot population-and-parity protocol yields fixed-phase GHZ+ fidelity of 99.8960%, an estimated standard error of 0.2885 percentage points and a conservative physical 95% interval of [98.2342%, 100%]. Timing metrics are partial and do not establish quantum advantage. Scaling to 9,984 processor-level logical qubits is an engineering target, distinct from the demonstrated register.
summary: This paper reports on Zeus-256, a 256-qubit room-temperature NV-diamond quantum processor featuring a novel, optically programmable biomolecular quantum bus. The system was benchmarked across numerous quantum algorithms, demonstrating high fidelity in entanglement generation and factoring large numbers. It represents a significant step toward scalable, solid-state quantum computation by integrating multiple physical control mechanisms.
main_problem: Developing scalable quantum processors that can simultaneously address qubit coherence, control fidelity, readout, inter-qubit connectivity, and overall system complexity.
main_result: The authors demonstrated a 256-qubit room-temperature NV-diamond processor capable of running complex algorithms, achieving high fidelity in GHZ state preparation and factorizing 84-bit numbers.
method: The system executes OpenQASM 2.0 circuits, transpiling them into sequences controlling microwave, RF, optical, and biomolecular bus configurations.
model_or_system: The platform is Zeus-256, a room-temperature NV-diamond processor where each logical qubit combines an NV electron-spin ensemble with nuclear-spin memory. Connectivity is mediated by a proprietary, optically programmable biomolecular quantum bus.
key_observables: Bell-CHSH value ($S = 2.8008 \pm 0.0446$), GHZ+ fidelity (99.8960%), Grover search success rate (93.55%), and successful factor recovery for 8-84 bit integers.
important_parameters: 256 simultaneously active processor-level logical qubits in a $16 	imes 16$ array; execution time of 551.694 ms for the 84-bit endpoint.
main_assumptions: The biomolecular bus provides reconfigurable long-range interactions, but the timing metrics do not establish quantum advantage, and the 9,984-qubit scale is an engineering target.
paper_structure: The paper details the architecture, benchmarking across heterogeneous circuits (QFT, Grover, Shor, etc.), reporting quantitative results for entanglement fidelity and computational tasks.
why_interesting: The integration of a solid-state spin system (NV-diamond) with a bio-inspired, optically programmable quantum bus offers a novel, highly scalable pathway for realizing long-range connectivity in quantum computation, bridging solid-state physics with molecular engineering.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Processor-level architecture of Zeus-256, showing the NV-diamond substrate, optical excitation/programming/readout, MW and RF control, the optically programmable biomolecular quantum-bus coupling layer, measurement electronics, bias field, timing/synchronization, RFSoC pulse orchestration, and the feedback controller. The biomolecular layer contains the internal protein–chromophore triplet-spin mediator described in Sections 3.3 and 4; it is an interaction resource and not an additional user-exposed qubit register.

Figure 2: Demonstrated Zeus-256 logical-qubit hierarchy and engineering scale-up path to Zeus-9984. The demonstrated 16 × 16 Zeus-256 register and one processor-level logical-qubit field are shown together with the optically programmable biomolecular quantum-bus coupling layer, which contains an internal metastable electronic triplet-spin mediator and provides effective local and long-range interaction pathways for compiled circuits. The figure also shows the principal engineering tasks associated with scaling the same architecture toward the target of 9,984 processor-level logical qubits.

Figure 3: Processor-level schematic of the Zeus biomolecular quantum bus. The optically programmable biomolecular layer contains a proprietary protein–chromophore spin system similar to EYFP, incorporating a metastable electronic triplet spin degree of freedom used internally as part of the quantum bus. This molecular spin subsystem is an interaction mediator and is not exposed as an additional processor-level logical-qubit register. Optical programming changes the dielectric and coupling state of the biomolecular layer, while synchronized MW/RF control and fluorescence readout operate on selected NV-diamond processor-level logical qubits.
